questions.q: A strong discursive essay
o: answers the exact question with a clear, sustained line of argument
lists everything known about the topic
questions.why: Relevance and a sustained argument earn the top marks.

questions.q: Counter-arguments should be
o: raised and then evaluated or rebutted
given as much support as your own view without judgement
questions.why: Evaluation shows balance and judgement.

questions.q: A good conclusion
o: reaches a justified judgement on the question
repeats the introduction word for word
questions.why: It should follow from the argument.

long.q: 'Social media does more harm than good to young people.' How far do you agree? (Plan and write in 75 minutes; mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a clear position that answers 'how far', stated early
B1: at least three developed arguments, each with specific evidence
B1: a logical structure with linked paragraphs
B1: a reasoned conclusion that follows from the argument
B1: accurate, fluent and varied language

topics.name: Economic, historical, moral, political and social topics

questions.q: Which is the best evidence to support a claim in a GP essay?
o: a specific, relevant example with context
questions.why: Precise examples make arguments convincing.

questions.q: An essay asks if a country should help poorer nations. What keeps it relevant?
o: Discussing the country-level argument the question asks about
Writing about rich individuals giving to charity
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some focused on rich individuals instead of the country context.

questions.q: How should you choose an essay question?
o: Pick the topic you know most facts about
By how well you can answer that question, not just how much you know about the topic
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many chose familiar topics they couldn't answer well.

questions.q: An essay on whether technology isolates people should
o: weigh different kinds of technology and contexts
questions.why: Qualified, nuanced judgements score well.

questions.q: Which shows a balanced argument?
o: Weighing evidence on both sides and reaching a reasoned judgement
questions.why: Measured, supported points do better than sweeping claims.

questions.q: Why avoid sweeping generalisations like 'everyone has a mobile'?
o: They are inaccurate and weaken the argument
questions.why: Examiners (2023): unsupported generalisations were common.

long.q: Evaluate the claim that governments, not individuals, should take the lead in tackling climate change. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: defines the scope (which governments, which individuals)
B1: argues the case for government action with examples
B1: argues the case for individual action with examples
B1: weighs the two and reaches a judgement
B1: clear structure and accurate expression

topics.name: Literature, language, the arts and media

questions.q: 'To what extent' questions require
o: a judgement on how far you agree
questions.why: They ask for degree, not just a side.

questions.q: Which is more suitable in a formal essay?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): avoid contractions and informal words.

questions.q: What is the best way to use advanced vocabulary?
o: Only where it is precise and correctly used
questions.why: Examiners (2023): complex words were sometimes used wrongly.

questions.q: 'Explain in your own words' means
o: paraphrase the meaning without lifting key words
questions.why: Lifting shows no understanding.

questions.q: When asked to answer in your own words, you should:
o: Rephrase without reusing the key words of the text
questions.why: Examiners (2023): reusing the original words lost credit.

questions.q: A question asks about disadvantages for one person. What loses marks?
o: Writing about advantages or about other people
questions.why: Answer exactly the angle the question sets.

questions.q: When evaluating a source's reliability, consider
o: its author, purpose, evidence and date
questions.why: These affect how far it can be trusted.

questions.q: A correlation in data shows
o: that two things vary together, not necessarily cause and effect
proof that one causes the other
questions.why: Correlation is not causation.

questions.q: What turns a point into a developed point?
o: Explaining its likely impact or consequence
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some developments just restated the evidence.

long.q: A passage claims a new school timetable 'improved results' because exam averages rose the following year. Identify two weaknesses in this reasoning.
scheme: B1: correlation is not causation: other factors may have changed
B1: one year's data is too little to show a trend
B1: a different cohort sat the exams, so results aren't directly comparable
B1: no information on how big the rise was or whether it is significant

questions.q: Which is grammatically correct?
o: Neither the teacher nor the students were late.
Neither the teacher or the students was late.
Neither the teacher nor the students was late, and.
Neither of the teacher nor students were late.
questions.why: Neither…nor; the verb agrees with the nearer subject (students → were).

questions.q: In a summary, what should you avoid?
o: Copying long phrases and adding your own opinions
questions.why: Precision matters: choose words that keep the original meaning.

questions.q: Why must synonyms be chosen carefully?
o: A near-synonym can change the meaning
questions.why: Examiners (2023): 'easily' was a poor substitute for 'contactlessly'.
